summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation, in which the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist was formally entered on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024. The designation has produced arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges.

The federal law of July 2023 banning gender transition outright, both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition, applies in Moscow as it does nationwide.

Enforcement in Moscow has been direct. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution records that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life in Russia that year, and that Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024.

Public assembly is not available. Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.
tangentialFactors:
Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation was reported in February 2025 in a case concerning organising, following a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025. The sentence shows that the extremism provisions carry custodial exposure, not only fines.

In 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail," a statement that indicates registry-level refusal rather than a statutory prohibition alone.
localsOnly:
For Moscow residents, the practical consequences of the 2023 federal ban on gender transition include the loss of any route to legal gender recognition and of access to gender-affirming surgery, alongside the voiding of marriages and loss of adoption rights described in the national framework.

Residents face the extremism designation directly: the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024, and gay bar owners in the city have been arrested on extremism charges.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Moscow Registry Office currently refuses same-sex marriage petitions is unresolved in the sources; the only sourced statement is a 2011 remark by the then-head of the office that such attempts are "doomed to fail."

The outcome of Kotov's case after his late December 2024 arrest is not sourced here.

No Moscow-specific data on fines under the propaganda statutes, on hate-crime reporting, or on detention conditions is present in the inventory; those layers are carried by the national record.
